title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
This page is a pure numerical worksheet. It continues §36 of E510, where Euler sums two power series, Q and Q′, for one trial value of the load parameter t. Since l t = 2,3010300, the trial value is t = 200. The formulas come from §33, which is not on this page; the series presumably serve the boundary/stability condition for a heavy column buckling under its own weight.

The rule can be recovered from the logarithms. For each term Euler adds l t = 2,3010300 to the logarithm of the previous term and subtracts the logarithm of a divisor d_k:
- 1,9242793 = log 84
- 2,1663314 = log 146,667 = log(440/3)
- 2,3569815 = log 227,5
- 2,5137501 = log 326,4
- 2,6467304 = log 443,33
- 2,7621424 = log 578,29
- From the previous and next pages: d_1 = 40, d_8 = 731,25, ...

All of these fit d_k = (3k+1)(3k+2)(k+1)/k. The first term is I = t/6 = 33,3333. So the terms obey
Q_{k+1}/Q_k = −t·k/((k+1)(3k+1)(3k+2)),
or equivalently (k+1)Q_{k+1}/(kQ_k) = −t/((3k+1)(3k+2)). Thus kQ_k are coefficients of a series in powers of t (i.e. t x^3 at x = 1) with the Airy/Bessel-of-order-±1/3 denominators (3k+1)(3k+2), which is the structure that arises for the heavy column.

The primed series is Q′_k = Q_k/(3k+1):
- I′ = I/4
- II′ = II/7
- III′ = III/10
- IV′ = IV/13
- V′ = V/16
- VI′ = VI/19
- VII′ = VII/22
- VIII′ = VIII/25
This is what one obtains by integrating x^{3k} from 0 to 1, so Q′ is an integral of the Q-type function.

The second number in each column is the running partial sum. Because t = 200 is large, the terms alternate in sign and grow to about 541 before decaying. The partial sums therefore show severe cancellation, ending (next page) near Q ≈ 2,7284 and Q′ ≈ 1,498. Combined with P ≈ 0,1734 and P′ ≈ 0,1631 from §35, these presumably enter Euler's criterion for the critical height.

All logarithms, antilogarithms and partial sums on this page check correctly:
- 33,3333 − 166,6667 = −133,3334
- −133,3334 + 396,8254 = 263,4920
- 263,4920 − 541,1255 = −277,6335
- and so on down to −7,3898
- Q′ partial sums: −15,4762, 24,2063, −17,4187, 12,3135, −3,0282, 2,9491, 1,1299.
errors: No arithmetic errors on this page; every logarithm, antilogarithm and partial sum checks to the printed precision.

Methodological caveat: with t = 200 the alternating terms reach about 5·10^2, while the final sums are of order 1. Four-decimal values carry the answer, but the cancellation (loss of 2–3 significant digits) makes the results sensitive to rounding. Euler does not remark on this.

Historically, Euler's 1778 treatments of the heavy column are generally reported (e.g. by Truesdell) not to have reached the correct critical height later found by Greenhill (1881). The defect lies in the setup and criterion in other sections, not in this arithmetic. I am unsure of the precise diagnosis for E510 specifically.

ideas.what: Power-series solution of the heavy-column deflection equation, with term ratios −t·k/((k+1)(3k+1)(3k+2)) and integrated companion series Q′_k = Q_k/(3k+1)
